title: Hindi grammar
about: From your very first conversation to everyday Hindi, one short lesson at a time. Each lesson gives you something you can say straight away, then the grammar that makes it work. You don't need to know any grammar: each grammar word is explained when you first need it. Every example is everyday Hindi as it is spoken in India, written in Devanagari, with a reading in Latin letters.

lessons.title: Say hello and who you are
lessons.summary: Greet someone, say your name and where you're from, and ask them the same: your first Hindi conversation.
lessons.topic: The verb at the end; {{मैं … हूँ|maĩ … hū̃}} “I am”, {{है|hai}} “is”; {{से|se}} “from” after the place

goal.t: नमस्ते, मैं सारा हूँ। मैं अमेरिका से हूँ।
goal.r: namaste, maĩ sārā hū̃. maĩ amerikā se hū̃.
goal.tr: Hello, I'm Sarah. I'm from America.

dialog.t: मैं अमेरिका से हूँ। और आप?
dialog.r: maĩ amerikā se hū̃. aur āp?

blocks.p: Look at where the verb goes: at the very end. {{मैं सारा हूँ|maĩ sārā hū̃}} is, word for word, “I Sarah am”, and {{मैं अमेरिका से हूँ|maĩ amerikā se hū̃}} is “I America from am”. In Hindi the verb comes last, and everything else comes before it.

blocks.means: a group of words that says something complete: I'm from Delhi.
a word for doing or being: go, eat, am, is.

blocks.p: **Am and is.** {{हूँ|hū̃}} “am” goes only with {{मैं|maĩ}} “I”. {{है|hai}} “is” goes with one person or thing: {{मेरा नाम राहुल है|merā nām rāhul hai}} “My name is Rahul”. Rahul's question ends in {{हैं|haĩ}}: that is the polite “are” that goes with {{आप|āp}} “you” (the next lesson).

table: {{मैं सारा हूँ।|maĩ sārā hū̃.}} I'm Sarah.
{{मेरा नाम राहुल है।|merā nām rāhul hai.}} My name is Rahul.
{{आप कहाँ से हैं?|āp kahā̃ se haĩ?}} Where are you from?

blocks.p: **From.** {{से|se}} “from” comes *after* the place: {{दिल्ली से|dillī se}} “from Delhi”. All of Hindi's little words for “in”, “on”, “from” come after the word they belong to (lesson 8).

ex.note: Hindi needs no word for “a”: “I doctor am”.
a set phrase: learn it as it is

blocks.tip: **Reading the Latin letters.** A line over a vowel makes it long: ā as in “father”, ī as in “police”, ū as in “rule”; a short a sounds like the u in “but”. e is as in “they”, o as in “go”, ai like the e in “bed”. A wavy line (hū̃, haĩ) means the vowel is said through the nose. A dot under ṭ, ḍ, ṛ, ṇ means the tongue curls back. An h after a letter (kh, th, bh) is a puff of breath: th is a t with a puff, never the th of “the”. ch is as in “church”. Tap any example to hear it.

mistakes.why: The verb goes last: “I Sarah am”.
{{से|se}} “from” comes after the place.
The sentence is about “my name”, so “is”: {{है|hai}}. {{हूँ|hū̃}} goes only with {{मैं|maĩ}}.

options: {{मैं दिल्ली से हूँ।|maĩ dillī se hū̃.}}
{{मैं हूँ दिल्ली से।|maĩ hū̃ dillī se.}}
{{मैं से दिल्ली हूँ।|maĩ se dillī hū̃.}}
practice.why: The verb {{हूँ|hū̃}} goes last, and {{से|se}} after the place.

practice.q: You're Tom, from London. Choose your replies.

lines.why: {{से|se}} comes after the place: {{लंदन से|landan se}} “from London”.

answers.r: namaste, maĩ jôn hū̃. maĩ amerikā se hū̃.

answers.tr: Hello, my name is Emma. I'm from Canada.

lessons.title: Talk to people with respect
lessons.summary: Choose the right “you” (आप, तुम or तू) and ask “How are you?”: Hindi shows respect in every sentence.
lessons.topic: {{आप|āp}}, {{तुम|tum}}, {{तू|tū}} “you”, with {{हैं|haĩ}}, {{हो|ho}}, {{है|hai}}; {{हम|ham}} “we”; {{जी|jī}}

goal.t: नमस्ते जी, आप कैसे हैं?
goal.r: namaste jī, āp kaise haĩ?
goal.tr: Hello, how are you?
goal.note: to a man; to a woman: {{आप कैसी हैं?|āp kaisī haĩ?}}

dialog.t: मैं ठीक हूँ, शुक्रिया। आप कैसी हैं?
dialog.r: maĩ ṭhīk hū̃, shukriyā. āp kaisī haĩ?
dialog.tr: I'm fine, thank you. How are you?

blocks.p: Tom says “you” in two different ways: {{आप|āp}} to his older colleague, {{तुम|tum}} to his friend Ravi. Hindi has three words for “you”, and you choose by who you are talking to.

blocks.means: a short word that stands for a person or a thing: I, you, he, she, we.

table: anyone you don't know well, anyone older, anyone you respect: the safe choice
friends, people your age, younger people
a very close friend, a small child (rude to anyone else)

blocks.p: **Each “you” has its own “are”.** {{आप|āp}} goes with {{हैं|haĩ}}, {{तुम|tum}} with {{हो|ho}}, {{तू|tū}} with {{है|hai}}. Hindi speakers hear the difference at once, so keep each pair together. {{हम|ham}} “we” takes {{हैं|haĩ}} too: {{हम दोस्त हैं|ham dost haĩ}} “We're friends”.

**When in doubt, say {{आप|āp}}.** Being too polite is never a mistake, while {{तू|tū}} to a stranger is an insult. For even more respect, add {{जी|jī}} after a name or a title: {{शर्मा जी|sharmā jī}} “Mr (or Mrs) Sharma”, {{जी हाँ|jī hā̃}} “yes” (politely).

ex.note: to a man; to a woman: {{आप कैसी हैं?|āp kaisī haĩ?}}

ex.t: शर्मा जी, आप कहाँ से हैं?
ex.r: sharmā jī, āp kahā̃ se haĩ?
ex.tr: Mrs Sharma, where are you from?

ex.note: to a very close friend or a child

blocks.tip: {{नमस्ते|namaste}} works at any time of day, for “hello” and for “goodbye”. {{शुक्रिया|shukriyā}} and {{धन्यवाद|dhanyavād}} both mean “thank you”; the second is a little more formal.

mistakes.why: {{आप|āp}} goes with {{हैं|haĩ}}. ({{हो|ho}} is the “are” of {{तुम|tum}}.)
{{तुम|tum}} goes with {{हो|ho}}.

lines.r: maĩ bhī ṭhīk hū̃. āp kahā̃ se haĩ?

lessons.title: Ask yes-or-no questions and say no
lessons.summary: Ask “Are you…?”, answer yes or no, ask who, what and where, and say what you are not.
lessons.topic: {{क्या|kyā}} at the start of a question; {{जी हाँ|jī hā̃}}, {{जी नहीं|jī nahī̃}}; {{नहीं|nahī̃}} before the verb; {{कौन|kaun}}, {{क्या|kyā}}, {{कहाँ|kahā̃}}, {{कैसे|kaise}}

goal.t: जी नहीं, मैं डॉक्टर नहीं हूँ। मैं टीचर हूँ।
goal.r: jī nahī̃, maĩ ḍôkṭar nahī̃ hū̃. maĩ ṭīchar hū̃.
goal.tr: No, I'm not a doctor. I'm a teacher.

dialog.t: जी नहीं, मैं डॉक्टर नहीं हूँ। मैं टीचर हूँ।
dialog.r: jī nahī̃, maĩ ḍôkṭar nahī̃ hū̃. maĩ ṭīchar hū̃.
dialog.tr: No, I'm not a doctor. I'm a teacher.

dialog.t: अच्छा! क्या आप इंग्लैंड से हैं?
dialog.r: achchhā! kyā āp iṅglaiṇḍ se haĩ?

dialog.t: जी हाँ, मैं लंदन से हूँ। और आप?
dialog.r: jī hā̃, maĩ landan se hū̃. aur āp?
dialog.tr: Yes, I'm from London. And you?

dialog.t: मैं यहीं से हूँ, दिल्ली से।
dialog.r: maĩ yahī̃ se hū̃, dillī se.
dialog.tr: I'm from right here, from Delhi.

blocks.p: **Yes-or-no questions.** Put {{क्या|kyā}} at the start and let your voice rise at the end: {{आप डॉक्टर हैं।|āp ḍôkṭar haĩ.}} “You're a doctor.” → {{क्या आप डॉक्टर हैं?|kyā āp ḍôkṭar haĩ?}} “Are you a doctor?” Nothing else changes: the words keep their order and the verb stays last. In everyday speech the {{क्या|kyā}} is often left out, and only the voice rises.
**Yes and no.** {{हाँ|hā̃}} is “yes”, {{नहीं|nahī̃}} is “no”; with {{जी|jī}} in front they become polite: {{जी हाँ|jī hā̃}}, {{जी नहीं|jī nahī̃}}.
**Not.** {{नहीं|nahī̃}} also means “not”. It goes just before the verb: {{मैं डॉक्टर नहीं हूँ।|maĩ ḍôkṭar nahī̃ hū̃.}} “I'm not a doctor.”

blocks.means: a word that asks for information: who, what, where, how.

blocks.p: **Who, what, where.** A question word stands where the answer would be, so the order doesn't change: {{आप कहाँ से हैं?|āp kahā̃ se haĩ?}} “Where are you from?”, word for word “you where from are?”, and the answer {{मैं दिल्ली से हूँ।|maĩ dillī se hū̃.}} fills the same place. Inside a sentence, {{क्या|kyā}} means “what”: {{आपका नाम क्या है?|āpkā nām kyā hai?}} “What's your name?”

table: {{आपका नाम क्या है?|āpkā nām kyā hai?}}

ex.t: क्या आप मुंबई से हैं? — नहीं, पुणे से।
ex.r: kyā āp mumbaī se haĩ? — nahī̃, puṇe se.
ex.tr: Are you from Mumbai? — No, from Pune.
ex.note: a short answer can leave the verb out

mistakes.why: {{नहीं|nahī̃}} goes just before the verb.
Hindi doesn't swap words to make a question, as English does: {{क्या|kyā}} at the start, and the verb stays last.

lessons.title: Ask for what you need
lessons.summary: Order at a café or a tea stall, and say what you need: “I'd like a tea and a samosa.”
lessons.topic: {{मुझे … चाहिए|mujhe … chāhie}} “I need, I'd like”; {{… दीजिए|… dījie}} “… please”; {{और|aur}} “and”, {{भी|bhī}} “too”

goal.t: मुझे एक चाय और एक समोसा चाहिए।
goal.r: mujhe ek chāy aur ek samosā chāhie.
goal.tr: I'd like a tea and a samosa.

blocks.p: **I need, I'd like.** {{मुझे … चाहिए|mujhe … chāhie}} is how you ask for things in Hindi. Word for word it is “to me … is needed”: {{मुझे|mujhe}} means “to me”, {{चाहिए|chāhie}} “is needed”, and the thing goes in between. It is polite enough for any shop or café, and it covers “I want”, “I need” and “I'd like”.
**Please give.** {{दीजिए|dījie}} “please give” goes after the thing: {{एक चाय दीजिए|ek chāy dījie}} “A tea, please.” (It is the polite form of {{देना|denā}} “to give”: lesson 12.)

**Asking someone else.** To ask what someone needs, {{मुझे|mujhe}} “to me” becomes {{आपको|āpko}} “to you”: {{आपको क्या चाहिए?|āpko kyā chāhie?}} “What would you like?” And {{नहीं|nahī̃}} goes just before {{चाहिए|chāhie}} (lesson 3).

table: {{मुझे चीनी नहीं चाहिए।|mujhe chīnī nahī̃ chāhie.}}

ex.note: {{भी|bhī}} “too, also” comes right after the word it is about: “me too”

blocks.tip: {{एक|ek}} means “one”, and it is how you say “a” when you count or order: {{एक चाय|ek chāy}} “a (one) tea”. Hindi has no word for “the”.

mistakes.why: With {{चाहिए|chāhie}}, the person is “to me”: {{मुझे|mujhe}}, not {{मैं|maĩ}}.
{{भी|bhī}} comes after the word it is about: “me too” is {{मुझे भी|mujhe bhī}}.

lessons.title: Point at things and people
lessons.summary: Ask “What's this?” and “Who's that?”, and say “That's my friend.”
lessons.topic: {{यह|yah}} “this”, {{वह|vah}} “that”; {{ये|ye}}, {{वे|ve}} “these, those”; {{वह|vah}} is also “he, she, it”

goal.t: यह क्या है? और वह कौन है?
goal.r: yah kyā hai? aur vah kaun hai?
goal.tr: What's this? And who's that?

dialog.t: यह लस्सी है। बहुत अच्छी है!
dialog.r: yah lassī hai. bahut achchhī hai!

blocks.p: **This and that.** {{यह|yah}} is “this” (near you), {{वह|vah}} is “that” (further away). With {{है|hai}} they make the most useful sentences there are: {{यह क्या है?|yah kyā hai?}} “What's this?”, {{वह कौन है?|vah kaun hai?}} “Who's that?” {{क्या|kyā}} “what” is for things, {{कौन|kaun}} “who” for people.

**He, she, it.** Hindi has no separate words for “he”, “she” and “it”: {{वह|vah}} is all of them (and {{यह|yah}} for someone near). {{वह डॉक्टर है|vah ḍôkṭar hai}} can be “he's a doctor” or “she's a doctor”: the situation tells you which.

**These and those.** For more than one: {{ये|ye}} “these, they (near)” and {{वे|ve}} “those, they”, with {{हैं|haĩ}}: {{वे मेरे दोस्त हैं|ve mere dost haĩ}} “They're my friends.” In speech you'll hear {{ये|ye}} for {{यह|yah}} too, and {{वो|vo}} for both {{वह|vah}} and {{वे|ve}}: that is how most people say them.

ex.note: {{मेरी|merī}} “my” shows that the friend is a woman (lesson 10)

mistakes.why: More than one: {{हैं|haĩ}}.
For a person, “who”: {{कौन|kaun}}. {{क्या|kyā}} is for things.

options: He's a doctor, or she's a doctor

lessons.title: Say what people and things are like
lessons.summary: Describe people, food and places (“The food is very good”), and meet Hindi's two genders.
lessons.topic: Masculine and feminine nouns; adjectives in {{-आ|-ā}} / {{-ई|-ī}}; adjectives that never change; {{बहुत|bahut}} “very”

goal.t: खाना बहुत अच्छा है, और चाय भी अच्छी है।
goal.r: khānā bahut achchhā hai, aur chāy bhī achchhī hai.
goal.tr: The food is very good, and the tea is good too.

blocks.p: Look at “good” in the goal sentence: {{अच्छा|achchhā}} with {{खाना|khānā}} “food”, but {{अच्छी|achchhī}} with {{चाय|chāy}} “tea”. The word for “good” changes because food and tea are different genders in Hindi.

blocks.means: a word for a person, a thing or a place: friend, tea, Delhi.
in Hindi, every noun is either masculine or feminine, things too: tea is feminine, food is masculine.
a word that describes a noun: big, good, hot.

blocks.p: **Two kinds of nouns.** For people, the gender follows the person: {{लड़का|laṛkā}} “boy” is masculine, {{लड़की|laṛkī}} “girl” feminine. For things, a rule of thumb: nouns ending in {{-आ|-ā}} are mostly masculine ({{कमरा|kamrā}} “room”, {{खाना|khānā}} “food”), nouns ending in {{-ई|-ī}} mostly feminine ({{चाबी|chābī}} “key”, {{गाड़ी|gāṛī}} “car”). The others you learn with the word: {{चाय|chāy}} “tea” and {{किताब|kitāb}} “book” are feminine, {{घर|ghar}} “house” and {{शहर|shahar}} “city” masculine. (And a few break the rule: {{पानी|pānī}} “water” and {{आदमी|ādmī}} “man” are masculine.)

**Adjectives that change.** An adjective ending in {{-आ|-ā}} keeps {{-आ|-ā}} with a masculine noun and changes to {{-ई|-ī}} with a feminine one. It changes wherever it stands: before the noun ({{बड़ी गाड़ी|baṛī gāṛī}} “a big car”) or at the end of the sentence ({{गाड़ी बड़ी है|gāṛī baṛī hai}} “The car is big”).

**Adjectives that never change.** Adjectives that don't end in {{-आ|-ā}} stay the same for everyone: {{सुंदर|sundar}} “beautiful”, {{ख़ुश|khush}} “happy”, {{लाल|lāl}} “red”, {{मुश्किल|mushkil}} “difficult”, {{गरम|garam}} “hot”: {{सुंदर घर|sundar ghar}}, {{सुंदर गाड़ी|sundar gāṛī}}. {{बहुत|bahut}} “very” never changes either.

blocks.tip: With people, the adjective follows the person: {{राहुल लंबा है|rāhul lambā hai}} “Rahul is tall”, {{प्रिया लंबी है|priyā lambī hai}} “Priya is tall”. When you learn a new noun, learn its gender with it: {{चाय|chāy}} (feminine).

lessons.summary: Say “two rooms”, “three books”, “nice people”, and count to ten: Hindi plurals, which depend on gender.
lessons.topic: Plural nouns: {{-आ → -ए|-ā → -e}}, {{-ई → -इयाँ|-ī → -iyā̃}}, {{-एँ|-ẽ}}; adjectives in {{-ए|-e}}; numbers 1 to 10

blocks.means: the form of a word for more than one: book → books.

blocks.p: **Masculine nouns.** Those ending in {{-आ|-ā}} change it to {{-ए|-e}}: {{केला|kelā}} → {{केले|kele}} “bananas”, {{कमरा|kamrā}} → {{कमरे|kamre}} “rooms”. The other masculine nouns don't change at all: {{एक आम|ek ām}} “one mango”, {{चार आम|chār ām}} “four mangoes”; {{एक आदमी|ek ādmī}}, {{दो आदमी|do ādmī}}.

**Feminine nouns.** Those ending in {{-ई|-ī}} take {{-इयाँ|-iyā̃}}: {{लड़की|laṛkī}} → {{लड़कियाँ|laṛkiyā̃}} “girls”. The others add {{-एँ|-ẽ}}: {{किताब|kitāb}} → {{किताबें|kitābẽ}} “books”, {{बहन|bahan}} → {{बहनें|bahnẽ}} “sisters”.

**Adjectives** in {{-आ|-ā}} take {{-ए|-e}} with a masculine plural: {{बड़े कमरे|baṛe kamre}} “big rooms”, {{अच्छे लोग|achchhe log}} “nice people”. With a feminine plural they stay {{-ई|-ī}}: {{अच्छी किताबें|achchhī kitābẽ}} “good books”. And the verb becomes {{हैं|haĩ}}.

lessons.title: Say where things are
lessons.summary: Ask “Where is…?” and say “on the table”, “in the bag”, “near the station”.
lessons.topic: Postpositions after the noun: {{में|mẽ}}, {{पर|par}}, {{के पास|ke pās}}, {{के सामने|ke sāmne}}, {{के पीछे|ke pīchhe}}, {{के नीचे|ke nīche}}, {{के अंदर|ke andar}}; {{कहाँ|kahā̃}}

goal.t: मेरी चाबी कहाँ है? — मेज़ पर है।
goal.r: merī chābī kahā̃ hai? — mez par hai.
goal.tr: Where's my key? — It's on the table.

dialog.tr: No, it's not on the table.
Yes, it's in the bag. Thanks!

blocks.means: a little word that says where, when or how, like “in”, “on”, “from” in English, but placed after the noun: {{घर में|ghar mẽ}} “in the house”.

blocks.p: **After the noun.** English says “in the bag”; Hindi says “bag in”: {{बैग में|baig mẽ}}. Hindi's postpositions always come after their word: {{मेज़ पर|mez par}} “on the table”, {{दिल्ली से|dillī se}} “from Delhi” (lesson 1).

**Where is it?** {{कहाँ|kahā̃}} “where” takes the place of the answer: {{चाबी कहाँ है?|chābī kahā̃ hai?}} → {{चाबी मेज़ पर है।|chābī mez par hai.}} When it's clear what you're talking about, the answer can be just {{मेज़ पर|mez par}}.

table: {{स्टेशन के पास|sṭeshan ke pās}} near the station
{{होटल के सामने|hoṭal ke sāmne}} in front of the hotel
{{घर के पीछे|ghar ke pīchhe}} behind the house
{{मेज़ के नीचे|mez ke nīche}} under the table
{{गाड़ी के अंदर|gāṛī ke andar}} inside the car

blocks.p: **Two-word postpositions** start with {{के|ke}}: {{के पास|ke pās}}, {{के सामने|ke sāmne}}. The {{के|ke}} always stays: “near the station” is {{स्टेशन के पास|sṭeshan ke pās}}.

ex.tr: The key is in the bag.
The book is on the table.

ex.t: बैंक कहाँ है? — स्टेशन के पास।
ex.r: baiṅk kahā̃ hai? — sṭeshan ke pās.
ex.tr: Where's the bank? — Near the station.
The cat is under the bed.
The car is in front of the house.

blocks.tip: {{पर|par}} is “on”, and also “at” for some places: {{घर पर|ghar par}} “at home”, {{काम पर|kām par}} “at work”. For a town or a country, “in” is {{में|mẽ}}: {{मुंबई में|mumbaī mẽ}}.

mistakes.why: The postposition comes after its noun: “bag in”.

mistakes.tr: The bank is near the station.
mistakes.why: {{के पास|ke pās}} keeps its {{के|ke}}.

lessons.title: Talk about places in town
lessons.summary: Say “in the room”, “behind that door”, “with friends”: how Hindi words change before in, on and from.
lessons.topic: The oblique form: {{कमरा → कमरे में|kamrā → kamre mẽ}}; plurals in {{-ओं|-õ}}; {{इस|is}}, {{उस|us}} “this, that”

goal.t: मैं बड़े बाज़ार में हूँ, दोस्तों के साथ।
goal.r: maĩ baṛe bāzār mẽ hū̃, dostõ ke sāth.
goal.tr: I'm at the big market, with friends.

dialog.t: आपका कमरा दूसरी मंज़िल पर है।
dialog.r: āpkā kamrā dūsrī manzil par hai.
dialog.tr: Your room is on the second floor.

dialog.t: नाश्ता नीचे, छोटे कमरे में है।
dialog.r: nāshtā nīche, chhoṭe kamre mẽ hai.
dialog.tr: Breakfast is downstairs, in the small room.

dialog.t: लिफ़्ट उस दरवाज़े के पीछे है।
dialog.r: lifṭ us darvāze ke pīchhe hai.
dialog.tr: The elevator is behind that door.

blocks.p: Look at the receptionist's words: {{कमरा|kamrā}} “room” becomes {{कमरे में|kamre mẽ}} “in the room”, and {{दरवाज़ा|darvāzā}} “door” becomes {{दरवाज़े के पीछे|darvāze ke pīchhe}} “behind the door”. A word changes when a postposition comes after it.

blocks.means: the form a Hindi noun, adjective or pronoun takes before a postposition (in, on, from…): {{कमरा|kamrā}} “room”, but {{कमरे में|kamre mẽ}} “in the room”.

blocks.p: **Masculine nouns in {{-आ|-ā}}** change it to {{-ए|-e}} when a postposition follows: {{कमरे में|kamre mẽ}}, {{दरवाज़े पर|darvāze par}} “at the door”. Other nouns don't change in the singular: {{घर में|ghar mẽ}}, {{गाड़ी में|gāṛī mẽ}}, {{मेज़ पर|mez par}}.

**Adjectives and “this, that” follow.** An adjective in {{-आ|-ā}} also takes {{-ए|-e}} with a masculine noun: {{बड़ा बाज़ार|baṛā bāzār}} → {{बड़े बाज़ार में|baṛe bāzār mẽ}}. And {{यह|yah}}, {{वह|vah}} become {{इस|is}}, {{उस|us}}: {{उस दरवाज़े के पीछे|us darvāze ke pīchhe}} “behind that door”, {{इस शहर में|is shahar mẽ}} “in this city”.

**Plurals take {{-ओं|-õ}}.** Before a postposition, every plural noun ends in {{-ओं|-õ}}: {{दोस्तों के साथ|dostõ ke sāth}} “with friends”, {{कमरों में|kamrõ mẽ}} “in the rooms”, {{गाड़ियों में|gāṛiyõ mẽ}} “in the cars”. And {{ये|ye}}, {{वे|ve}} become {{इन|in}}, {{उन|un}}.

ex.tr: The children are in the room.

ex.t: स्टेशन इस सड़क के आख़िर में है।
ex.r: sṭeshan is saṛak ke ākhir mẽ hai.
ex.tr: The station is at the end of this road.

ex.t: मेरा बैग उस कुर्सी पर है।
ex.r: merā baig us kursī par hai.
ex.tr: My bag is on that chair.
The money is in that envelope.

lessons.title: Say whose it is, and talk about your family
lessons.summary: Say “my brother”, “Priya's car”, “for you”, and how old someone is.
lessons.topic: {{का / की / के|kā / kī / ke}} “'s, of”, which match the thing owned; {{मेरा|merā}}, {{आपका|āpkā}}, {{उसका|uskā}}…; {{मेरे साथ|mere sāth}}, {{आपके लिए|āpke lie}}; age

goal.t: यह मेरी बहन है। उसका नाम मीरा है।
goal.r: yah merī bahan hai. uskā nām mīrā hai.
goal.tr: This is my sister. Her name is Meera.

dialog.t: यह उसकी बेटी है। वह पाँच साल की है।
dialog.r: yah uskī beṭī hai. vah pā̃ch sāl kī hai.
dialog.tr: This is his daughter. She's five.

dialog.t: जी हाँ, ये मेरे माता-पिता हैं।
dialog.r: jī hā̃, ye mere mātā-pitā haĩ.

blocks.p: **'s and of.** {{का|kā}} works like English “'s”: {{प्रिया का घर|priyā kā ghar}} “Priya's house”. It is a postposition, so it comes after the owner. And it changes to match the **thing owned**, like an adjective in {{-आ|-ā}}:

table: {{राहुल का भाई|rāhul kā bhāī}} Rahul's brother
{{राहुल की बहन|rāhul kī bahan}} Rahul's sister
masculine plural, or before a postposition
{{राहुल के दोस्त|rāhul ke dost}} Rahul's friends

blocks.p: **My, your, his.** The words for “my”, “your” and so on change in the same way: {{मेरा भाई|merā bhāī}} “my brother”, {{मेरी बहन|merī bahan}} “my sister”, {{मेरे दोस्त|mere dost}} “my friends”.

**His or her?** {{उसका|uskā}} is both “his” and “her”: its ending tells you about the thing, not the owner. {{उसकी बहन|uskī bahan}} is “his sister” or “her sister”; {{उसका भाई|uskā bhāī}} is “his brother” or “her brother”. This is the opposite of English, so take your time with it.

**With me, for you.** Two-word postpositions start with {{के|ke}}, so with a pronoun they take the {{-ए|-e}} form: {{मेरे साथ|mere sāth}} “with me”, {{आपके लिए|āpke lie}} “for you”, {{उसके पास|uske pās}} “near him, near her”.

**Respect for elders.** Hindi speakers talk about parents, grandparents and teachers in the plural, as a mark of respect: {{मेरे पिता डॉक्टर हैं|mere pitā ḍôkṭar haĩ}} “My father is a doctor”, with {{मेरे|mere}} and {{हैं|haĩ}}, though it is one father.
**How old?** Age is said with {{का|kā}} too: {{मैं तीस साल का हूँ|maĩ tīs sāl kā hū̃}} “I'm thirty” (a man), {{मैं तीस साल की हूँ|maĩ tīs sāl kī hū̃}} (a woman), word for word “I am of thirty years”.

ex.t: यह मेरे दोस्त का घर है।

ex.t: मेरा बेटा सात साल का है।
ex.r: merā beṭā sāt sāl kā hai.

blocks.tip: {{तू|tū}} has its own “your”: {{तेरा|terā}}, {{तेरी|terī}}, {{तेरे|tere}}. And a few family words in {{-आ|-ā}} never take {{-ए|-e}}: {{पिता|pitā}} “father”, {{चाचा|chāchā}} “uncle”, {{दादा|dādā}} “grandfather”.

lessons.title: Say what you have and what there is
lessons.summary: Say “I have a bike”, “I have two brothers”, and ask “Is there a bank near here?”
lessons.topic: {{मेरे पास … है|mere pās … hai}} for things; {{मेरे दो भाई हैं|mere do bhāī haĩ}} for family; {{है|hai}} for “there is”; {{कोई|koī}}, {{कुछ|kuchh}}

goal.t: मेरे पास गाड़ी नहीं है, लेकिन मेरे पास साइकिल है।
goal.r: mere pās gāṛī nahī̃ hai, lekin mere pās sāikil hai.
goal.tr: I don't have a car, but I have a bike.

dialog.t: नहीं, मेरे पास गाड़ी नहीं है, लेकिन मेरे भाई के पास है।
dialog.r: nahī̃, mere pās gāṛī nahī̃ hai, lekin mere bhāī ke pās hai.
dialog.tr: No, I don't have a car, but my brother has one.
How many brothers do you have?

dialog.t: मेरे दो भाई हैं, और एक बहन।
dialog.r: mere do bhāī haĩ, aur ek bahan.
dialog.tr: I have two brothers, and a sister.

dialog.t: अच्छा! यहाँ पास में कोई पेट्रोल पंप है?
dialog.r: achchhā! yahā̃ pās mẽ koī peṭrol pamp hai?
dialog.tr: OK! Is there a gas station near here?

dialog.t: हाँ, स्टेशन के पास एक है।
dialog.r: hā̃, sṭeshan ke pās ek hai.
dialog.tr: Yes, there's one near the station.

blocks.p: **I have.** Hindi has no verb “to have” for things. It says “near me is”: {{मेरे पास गाड़ी है|mere pās gāṛī hai}}, word for word “near me car is”. The owner goes before {{के पास|ke pās}} ({{मेरे पास|mere pās}}, {{आपके पास|āpke pās}}, {{उसके पास|uske pās}}, {{राहुल के पास|rāhul ke pās}}), and the verb agrees with the thing: {{मेरे पास दो पेन हैं|mere pās do pen haĩ}} “I have two pens”.

**Family and friends** aren't “near you”: they are “yours”. {{मेरे दो भाई हैं|mere do bhāī haĩ}} “I have two brothers”, word for word “my two brothers are”; {{उसकी एक बेटी है|uskī ek beṭī hai}} “He (or she) has a daughter”.

**There is, there are.** {{है|hai}} and {{हैं|haĩ}} alone also mean “there is”, “there are”. Put the place first: {{कमरे में टीवी है|kamre mẽ ṭīvī hai}} “There's a TV in the room”, {{यहाँ बहुत लोग हैं|yahā̃ bahut log haĩ}} “There are a lot of people here”.

**Any, some.** {{कोई|koī}} is “some, any” for one person or thing; {{कुछ|kuchh}} is “something, anything, some”: {{क्या यहाँ कोई होटल है?|kyā yahā̃ koī hoṭal hai?}} “Is there a hotel here?”, {{मेरे पास कुछ पैसे हैं|mere pās kuchh paise haĩ}} “I have some money.”

table: {{मेरे पास गाड़ी है।|mere pās gāṛī hai.}}
{{मेरी एक बहन है।|merī ek bahan hai.}}
{{यहाँ एक बैंक है।|yahā̃ ek baiṅk hai.}}

ex.r: kyā āpke pās chhuṭṭe paise haĩ?

There are two beds in the room.

Before {{पास|pās}}, it is always {{मेरे|mere}}.
The verb agrees with the things: two pens, {{हैं|haĩ}}.

The verb agrees with the things: two tickets, {{हैं|haĩ}}.

practice.tr: There are two beds in the room.

practice.q: Looking for a hotel. Choose your questions.

क्या यहाँ पास में कोई होटल हूँ?
rs: kyā yahā̃ pās mẽ koī hoṭal hai?
kyā yahā̃ pās mẽ koī hoṭal hū̃?

lines.r: hā̃, bāzār mẽ do hoṭal haĩ.
lines.tr: Yes, there are two hotels in the market.

practice.q: Your turn: say one or two things you have (or don't have), and how many brothers or sisters you have.

answers.t: मेरे पास एक कुत्ता है। मेरी दो बहनें हैं।

lessons.title: Ask people to do things, and give directions
lessons.summary: Say “Please sit down”, “Come in”, “Don't worry”, and give or follow directions.
lessons.topic: Commands for {{आप|āp}} ({{-इए|-ie}}), {{तुम|tum}} ({{-ओ|-o}}) and {{तू|tū}} (the stem); {{दीजिए|dījie}}, {{लीजिए|lījie}}, {{कीजिए|kījie}}, {{पीजिए|pījie}}; {{मत|mat}} “don't”

goal.t: आइए, बैठिए! चाय पीजिए।
goal.r: āie, baiṭhie! chāy pījie.
goal.tr: Come in, sit down! Have some tea.

dialog.t: हाँ, और पुल के बाद दाएँ मुड़िए। स्टेशन वहीं है।
dialog.r: hā̃, aur pul ke bād dāẽ muṛie. sṭeshan vahī̃ hai.
dialog.tr: Yes, and after the bridge turn right. The station's right there.

blocks.means: what is left of a Hindi verb when you take off its {{-ना|-nā}}: {{बैठना|baiṭhnā}} “to sit” → {{बैठ|baiṭh}}.

blocks.p: **Three “you”s, three commands.** A Hindi verb is listed with {{-ना|-nā}}: {{बैठना|baiṭhnā}} “to sit”. Take off {{-ना|-nā}} and you have its stem, {{बैठ|baiṭh}}. Then add the ending that goes with the “you” you would use (lesson 2): {{-इए|-ie}} for {{आप|āp}}, {{-ओ|-o}} for {{तुम|tum}}, nothing for {{तू|tū}}.

Four very common verbs have a special {{आप|āp}} form: {{दीजिए|dījie}} “please give”, {{लीजिए|lījie}} “please take”, {{कीजिए|kījie}} “please do” (you'll hear {{करिए|karie}} too) and {{पीजिए|pījie}} “please drink”. {{आइए|āie}} “come” is also how you welcome someone in, and {{लीजिए|lījie}} is “here you are”.
**Don't.** Put {{मत|mat}} just before the verb: {{मत जाओ|mat jāo}} “Don't go”, {{चिंता मत कीजिए|chintā mat kījie}} “Don't worry” (word for word “worry don't do”).
**Directions.** {{सीधे जाइए|sīdhe jāie}} “go straight”, {{बाएँ मुड़िए|bāẽ muṛie}} “turn left”, {{दाएँ मुड़िए|dāẽ muṛie}} “turn right”, {{रुकिए|rukie}} “stop, wait”.

ex.tr: Please give me a little water.

ex.note: to a friend or a child
to a friend; to someone you call {{आप|āp}}: {{चिंता मत कीजिए|chintā mat kījie}}

blocks.tip: A command with {{आप|āp}} already sounds like “please”. To catch someone's attention politely, say {{सुनिए|sunie}} “excuse me” (word for word “listen”), and {{माफ़ कीजिए|māf kījie}} is “excuse me” or “sorry”.

mistakes.why: With {{आप|āp}}, the ending is {{-इए|-ie}}. ({{बैठो|baiṭho}} goes with {{तुम|tum}}.)
{{मत|mat}} goes right before the verb, here {{करो|karo}}.
{{देना|denā}} has a special form: {{दीजिए|dījie}}.

practice.q: Your new boss walks into the room. How do you ask her to sit down?
Choose the polite form of {{देना|denā}} “to give”.

practice.why: With a command, “don't” is {{मत|mat}}. ({{नहीं|nahī̃}} is for statements: lesson 3.)

practice.q: A friend comes to your home. Choose what you say.

lines.why: To a friend: the {{तुम|tum}} forms, in {{-ओ|-o}}. ({{बैठ|baiṭh}} is only for a very close friend or a child.)

lines.tr: Thanks. Wow, it's a beautiful house!

options: चाय पियो, और मिठाई भी लो।
चाय पियो, और मिठाई भी लेओ।
rs: chāy piyo, aur miṭhāī bhī lo.
chāy piyo, aur miṭhāī bhī leo.

practice.q: Ask someone politely to speak a little slower.
Your turn: tell a visitor how to get from your door to the nearest shop, with {{आप|āp}} commands.

answers.t: सीधे जाइए, फिर दाएँ मुड़िए। दुकान बैंक के सामने है।
answers.r: sīdhe jāie, phir dāẽ muṛie. dukān baiṅk ke sāmne hai.
answers.tr: Go straight, then turn right. The shop is opposite the bank.

answers.t: बाएँ मुड़िए, और पुल के बाद रुकिए।
answers.r: bāẽ muṛie, aur pul ke bād rukie.
answers.tr: Turn left, and stop after the bridge.

lessons.title: Shop and ask the price
lessons.summary: Ask how much things cost and how many there are, and point to “the red one”.
lessons.topic: {{कितना / कितनी / कितने|kitnā / kitnī / kitne}}; {{का|kā}} for a price; {{वाला|vālā}} “the … one”; numbers to 100

goal.t: यह कितने का है? — सौ रुपये का।
goal.r: yah kitne kā hai? — sau rupye kā.
goal.tr: How much is this? — A hundred rupees.

dialog.t: बहुत महँगा है! और वह लाल वाला?
dialog.r: bahut mahãgā hai! aur vah lāl vālā?
dialog.tr: That's very expensive! And the red one?
OK, I'll take the red one.

blocks.p: **How much, how many?** {{कितना|kitnā}} is an adjective in {{-आ|-ā}}, so it changes with its noun: {{कितना पानी?|kitnā pānī?}} “how much water?”, {{कितनी चीनी?|kitnī chīnī?}} “how much sugar?”, {{कितने लोग?|kitne log?}} “how many people?”

**What's the price?** A price is said with {{का|kā}} “of”: {{यह कितने का है?|yah kitne kā hai?}} “How much is this?”, word for word “this of how much is?”, and the answer {{सौ रुपये का|sau rupye kā}} “(of) a hundred rupees”. {{का|kā}} matches the thing, as always (lesson 10): {{यह साड़ी कितने की है?|yah sāṛī kitne kī hai?}} “How much is this sari?”, {{ये आम कितने के हैं?|ye ām kitne ke haĩ?}} “How much are these mangoes?”

**The red one.** {{वाला|vālā}} after an adjective means “the … one”: {{लाल वाला|lāl vālā}} “the red one”, {{बड़ी वाली|baṛī vālī}} “the big one” (for something feminine). It changes like {{अच्छा|achchhā}}.

ex.tr: How much rice do you need?

ex.t: दो सौ रुपये? यह बहुत महँगा है!
ex.r: do sau rupye? yah bahut mahãgā hai!
ex.tr: Two hundred rupees? That's very expensive!

blocks.tip: Hindi numbers from 11 to 99 each have their own word (25 is {{पच्चीस|pachchīs}}), so learn the ones you need for prices as you meet them. At the end, ask {{कितना हुआ?|kitnā huā?}} “How much does that come to?”

mistakes.why: {{कितना|kitnā}} changes like an adjective: many people, {{कितने|kitne}}.
{{साड़ी|sāṛī}} is feminine: {{की|kī}}.

practice.q: At a market stall: choose your lines.

lines.tr: Come in, what would you like?

practice.q: Your turn: you're buying a shirt. Ask the price, say it's too expensive, and ask about another one.

answers.t: यह शर्ट कितने की है? बहुत महँगी है! और वह नीली वाली?
answers.r: yah sharṭ kitne kī hai? bahut mahãgī hai! aur vah nīlī vālī?
answers.tr: How much is this shirt? It's very expensive! And the blue one?

answers.t: वह बड़ा वाला कितने का है?
answers.r: vah baṛā vālā kitne kā hai?
answers.tr: How much is that big one?

lessons.title: Say what you do every day
lessons.summary: Talk about your routine: “I get up at seven and drink tea.”
lessons.topic: The {{-ना|-nā}} form and the stem; the present: {{-ता / -ती / -ते|-tā / -tī / -te}} + {{हूँ / है / हैं|hū̃ / hai / haĩ}}

goal.t: मैं हर सुबह चाय पीता हूँ।
goal.r: maĩ har subah chāy pītā hū̃.
goal.tr: I drink tea every morning.
goal.note: said by a man; a woman says {{मैं हर सुबह चाय पीती हूँ|maĩ har subah chāy pītī hū̃}}

dialog.t: मैं छह बजे उठती हूँ और योग करती हूँ।
dialog.r: maĩ chhah baje uṭhtī hū̃ aur yog kartī hū̃.
dialog.tr: I get up at six and do yoga.

dialog.t: मैं सात बजे उठता हूँ और कॉफ़ी पीता हूँ।
dialog.r: maĩ sāt baje uṭhtā hū̃ aur kôfī pītā hū̃.
dialog.tr: I get up at seven and drink coffee.

dialog.t: मेरे पति भी कॉफ़ी पीते हैं।
dialog.r: mere pati bhī kôfī pīte haĩ.

dialog.t: बच्चे दूध पीते हैं और स्कूल जाते हैं।
dialog.r: bachche dūdh pīte haĩ aur skūl jāte haĩ.
dialog.tr: The children drink milk and go to school.

blocks.p: Priya says {{उठती हूँ|uṭhtī hū̃}}, Tom says {{उठता हूँ|uṭhtā hū̃}}: the same verb, “get up”, with a different ending, because one is a woman and the other a man.

blocks.means: the dictionary form of a verb, “to …”. In Hindi it ends in {{-ना|-nā}}: {{पीना|pīnā}} “to drink”, {{उठना|uṭhnā}} “to get up”.
the form of a verb that shows when something happens: now, usually, before, later.

blocks.p: **The present, for what you usually do.** Take the stem ({{पीना|pīnā}} → {{पी|pī}}, lesson 12), add {{-ता|-tā}}, {{-ती|-tī}} or {{-ते|-te}}, and end with {{हूँ|hū̃}}, {{है|hai}}, {{हैं|haĩ}} or {{हो|ho}}. The {{-ता|-tā}} ending changes like an adjective in {{-आ|-ā}}: it shows whether the person is masculine or feminine, one or more.
{{आप|āp}}, {{तुम|tum}} and {{हम|ham}} always take {{-ते|-te}} (or {{-ती|-tī}} for women), even for one person: they count as plural. A group of women takes {{-ती हैं|-tī haĩ}}.

**Usually, not right now.** {{मैं चाय पीता हूँ|maĩ chāy pītā hū̃}} means “I drink tea” as a habit, not “I'm drinking tea right now” (that's lesson 17). Time words like {{हर दिन|har din}} “every day”, {{रोज़|roz}} “daily” and {{सुबह|subah}} “in the morning” usually come early in the sentence; the verb stays last.

ex.note: a man; a woman: {{रहती हूँ|rahtī hū̃}}

ex.t: मेरी बहन बैंक में काम करती है।
ex.r: merī bahan baiṅk mẽ kām kartī hai.
ex.tr: My sister works in a bank.

ex.t: वह बहुत अच्छा खाना बनाती है।
ex.r: vah bahut achchhā khānā banātī hai.

blocks.tip: Listen for the ending: {{-ता|-tā}}, {{-ती|-tī}} or {{-ते|-te}} often tells you who is being talked about, even when you missed the first word.

mistakes.why: The present needs both parts: {{पीता|pītā}} and {{हूँ|hū̃}}.
A woman is speaking. A woman says {{रहती|rahtī}}: the ending follows the speaker.
{{आप|āp}} counts as plural: {{-ते हैं|-te haĩ}}.

practice.q: A woman is speaking. Choose the right form.
{{मेरा भाई बैंक में काम करता है।|merā bhāī baiṅk mẽ kām kartā hai.}} means…
options: My brother works in a bank.
My brother is working at the bank right now.
My brother worked in a bank.
practice.why: {{-ता है|-tā hai}} is what someone usually does.

practice.tr: My sister works in a bank.

practice.q: A new colleague asks about you. Choose your replies (you're a man).

options: मैं स्टेशन के पास रहता हूँ।
मैं स्टेशन के पास रहती हूँ।
rs: maĩ sṭeshan ke pās rahtā hū̃.
maĩ sṭeshan ke pās rahtī hū̃.

lines.t: और आप सुबह क्या पीते हैं, चाय या कॉफ़ी?
lines.r: aur āp subah kyā pīte haĩ, chāy yā kôfī?
lines.tr: And what do you drink in the morning, tea or coffee?

practice.q: Your turn: say three things you do every day. Watch the ending: {{-ता|-tā}} if you're a man, {{-ती|-tī}} if you're a woman.

answers.t: मैं सात बजे उठता हूँ, कॉफ़ी पीता हूँ और काम पर जाता हूँ।
answers.r: maĩ sāt baje uṭhtā hū̃, kôfī pītā hū̃ aur kām par jātā hū̃.
answers.tr: I get up at seven, drink coffee and go to work. (a man)

answers.t: मैं हर सुबह दौड़ती हूँ और फिर नाश्ता करती हूँ।
answers.r: maĩ har subah dauṛtī hū̃ aur phir nāshtā kartī hū̃.
answers.tr: Every morning I go for a run and then have breakfast. (a woman)

lessons.title: Ask about someone's day, and say what you don't do
lessons.summary: Ask “When do you get up?”, “Where do you work?”, and say “I don't eat meat”, “I never…”.
lessons.topic: Question words with the present ({{कब|kab}}, {{कहाँ|kahā̃}}, {{कैसे|kaise}}, {{क्यों|kyõ}}); {{नहीं|nahī̃}}, and the {{है|hai}} left out; {{हमेशा|hameshā}}, {{अक्सर|aksar}}, {{कभी-कभी|kabhī-kabhī}}, {{कभी नहीं|kabhī nahī̃}}

goal.t: मैं मांस नहीं खाता, लेकिन कभी-कभी मछली खाता हूँ।
goal.r: maĩ māns nahī̃ khātā, lekin kabhī-kabhī machhlī khātā hū̃.
goal.tr: I don't eat meat, but I sometimes eat fish.
goal.note: said by a man; a woman says {{खाती|khātī}}

dialog.t: मैं एक स्कूल में पढ़ाता हूँ।
dialog.r: maĩ ek skūl mẽ paṛhātā hū̃.

dialog.tr: How do you get to school?

dialog.t: मैं अक्सर बस से जाता हूँ। मेरे पास गाड़ी नहीं है।
dialog.r: maĩ aksar bas se jātā hū̃. mere pās gāṛī nahī̃ hai.
dialog.tr: I usually go by bus. I don't have a car.

dialog.t: और आप खाना कहाँ खाते हैं?
dialog.r: aur āp khānā kahā̃ khāte haĩ?

dialog.t: स्कूल में। मैं घर पर खाना नहीं बनाता!
dialog.r: skūl mẽ. maĩ ghar par khānā nahī̃ banātā!
dialog.tr: At school. I don't cook at home!

blocks.p: **Questions.** A question word goes where the answer would be (lesson 3): {{आप कहाँ काम करते हैं?|āp kahā̃ kām karte haĩ?}} “Where do you work?” → {{मैं बैंक में काम करता हूँ।|maĩ baiṅk mẽ kām kartā hū̃.}} For a yes-or-no question, {{क्या|kyā}} at the start: {{क्या आप हिंदी बोलते हैं?|kyā āp hindī bolte haĩ?}} “Do you speak Hindi?” Hindi has no “do” in questions: the verb is just the same as in the answer.

table: {{आप कब उठते हैं?|āp kab uṭhte haĩ?}} When do you get up?
{{तुम कहाँ रहते हो?|tum kahā̃ rahte ho?}} Where do you live?
{{आप क्या करते हैं?|āp kyā karte haĩ?}} What do you do?
{{आप काम पर कैसे जाते हैं?|āp kām par kaise jāte haĩ?}} How do you get to work?
{{तुम चाय क्यों नहीं पीते?|tum chāy kyõ nahī̃ pīte?}} Why don't you drink tea?

blocks.p: **Not.** {{नहीं|nahī̃}} goes before the verb, and in the present the {{हूँ / है / हैं|hū̃ / hai / haĩ}} at the end is usually left out: {{मैं मांस नहीं खाता|maĩ māns nahī̃ khātā}} “I don't eat meat”. (Keeping it, {{मैं मांस नहीं खाता हूँ|maĩ māns nahī̃ khātā hū̃}}, sounds more insistent.) The {{-ता / -ती / -ते|-tā / -tī / -te}} ending still shows who.

**How often.** {{हमेशा|hameshā}} “always”, {{अक्सर|aksar}} “often, usually”, {{कभी-कभी|kabhī-kabhī}} “sometimes”, and {{कभी … नहीं|kabhī … nahī̃}} “never”, with the {{नहीं|nahī̃}} before the verb: {{मैं कभी देर से नहीं उठता|maĩ kabhī der se nahī̃ uṭhtā}} “I never get up late.”

ex.tr: I sometimes go to the movies.
When do you get up in the morning?

ex.t: हम रविवार को काम नहीं करते।
ex.r: ham ravivār ko kām nahī̃ karte.

mistakes.why: {{नहीं|nahī̃}} goes just before the verb.
“Never” is {{कभी|kabhī}} with {{नहीं|nahī̃}}. {{कभी|kabhī}} alone means “ever” or “at some time”.

practice.q: Which one means “I don't drink coffee”?
options: {{मैं कॉफ़ी नहीं पीता।|maĩ kôfī nahī̃ pītā.}}
{{मैं नहीं कॉफ़ी पीता।|maĩ nahī̃ kôfī pītā.}}
{{नहीं मैं कॉफ़ी पीता।|nahī̃ maĩ kôfī pītā.}}
practice.why: {{नहीं|nahī̃}} just before the verb; the {{हूँ|hū̃}} can go.
In a statement: {{नहीं|nahī̃}}. ({{मत|mat}} is only for commands: lesson 12.)

practice.q: Meeting someone at a party. Choose your lines (you're a man).

lines.t: मैं अस्पताल में काम करता हूँ।
lines.r: maĩ aspatāl mẽ kām kartā hū̃.

lines.why: Asking what someone is: {{क्या आप … हैं?|kyā āp … haĩ?}}

lines.t: हाँ। और आप क्या करते हैं?
lines.r: hā̃. aur āp kyā karte haĩ?
lines.tr: Yes. And what do you do?

options: मैं एक कंपनी में काम करता हूँ।
मैं एक कंपनी में काम करता हैं।
rs: maĩ ek kampnī mẽ kām kartā hū̃.
maĩ ek kampnī mẽ kām kartā haĩ.

practice.q: Ask your friend Raj: “Why don't you drink tea?”
Your turn: say one thing you always do, one you sometimes do, and one you never do.

answers.t: मैं हमेशा सुबह कॉफ़ी पीता हूँ। मैं कभी-कभी दौड़ता हूँ। मैं कभी मांस नहीं खाता।
answers.r: maĩ hameshā subah kôfī pītā hū̃. maĩ kabhī-kabhī dauṛtā hū̃. maĩ kabhī māns nahī̃ khātā.
answers.tr: I always drink coffee in the morning. I sometimes go running. I never eat meat. (a man)

answers.t: मैं अक्सर दोस्तों के साथ खाना खाती हूँ, लेकिन मैं कभी टीवी नहीं देखती।
answers.r: maĩ aksar dostõ ke sāth khānā khātī hū̃, lekin maĩ kabhī ṭīvī nahī̃ dekhtī.
answers.tr: I often eat with friends, but I never watch TV. (a woman)

lessons.title: Say what you like
lessons.summary: Say “I like Hindi films”, “Do you like dancing?”, “She doesn't like coffee.”
lessons.topic: {{मुझे / आपको / उसे … पसंद है|mujhe / āpko / use … pasand hai}}; {{अच्छा लगता है|achchhā lagtā hai}}; the {{-ना|-nā}} form for activities ({{मुझे नाचना पसंद है|mujhe nāchnā pasand hai}})

goal.t: मुझे हिंदी फ़िल्में बहुत पसंद हैं।
goal.r: mujhe hindī filmẽ bahut pasand haĩ.
goal.tr: I really like Hindi films.

dialog.t: तुम्हें क्या पसंद है, चाय या कॉफ़ी?
dialog.r: tumhẽ kyā pasand hai, chāy yā kôfī?
dialog.tr: What do you like, tea or coffee?

dialog.t: मुझे चाय पसंद है। और तुम्हें?
dialog.r: mujhe chāy pasand hai. aur tumhẽ?

dialog.t: मुझे भी। क्या तुम्हें नाचना पसंद है?
dialog.r: mujhe bhī. kyā tumhẽ nāchnā pasand hai?
dialog.tr: Me too. Do you like dancing?

dialog.t: नहीं, मुझे नाचना पसंद नहीं है, लेकिन मुझे गाना अच्छा लगता है।
dialog.r: nahī̃, mujhe nāchnā pasand nahī̃ hai, lekin mujhe gānā achchhā lagtā hai.
dialog.tr: No, I don't like dancing, but I like singing.

blocks.p: **Liking works like needing.** Remember {{मुझे … चाहिए|mujhe … chāhie}} (lesson 4)? “I like” is built the same way: {{मुझे चाय पसंद है|mujhe chāy pasand hai}}, word for word “to me tea is liked”. The thing you like is what the sentence is about, so the verb agrees with it: {{मुझे हिंदी फ़िल्में पसंद हैं|mujhe hindī filmẽ pasand haĩ}}, with {{हैं|haĩ}} for the films.

blocks.means: the form of a person word that means “to …”: {{मुझे|mujhe}} “to me”, {{आपको|āpko}} “to you”, {{राहुल को|rāhul ko}} “to Rahul”. Hindi uses it for the person who needs, likes, feels or has to do something.

table: {{मुझे चाय पसंद है।|mujhe chāy pasand hai.}}
{{क्या आपको चाय पसंद है?|kyā āpko chāy pasand hai?}}
{{तुम्हें क्या पसंद है?|tumhẽ kyā pasand hai?}}
{{उसे कॉफ़ी पसंद नहीं है।|use kôfī pasand nahī̃ hai.}}
{{हमें यह शहर पसंद है।|hamẽ yah shahar pasand hai.}}
{{उन्हें क्रिकेट पसंद है।|unhẽ krikeṭ pasand hai.}}
{{राहुल को संगीत पसंद है।|rāhul ko saṅgīt pasand hai.}}

blocks.p: **Liking to do something.** Use the {{-ना|-nā}} form of the verb as the thing you like: {{मुझे नाचना पसंद है|mujhe nāchnā pasand hai}} “I like dancing”, {{उसे खाना बनाना पसंद है|use khānā banānā pasand hai}} “She likes cooking”.

**{{अच्छा लगना|achchhā lagnā}}.** Another way, a little warmer, is {{… अच्छा लगता है|… achchhā lagtā hai}}, “… seems good to me”: {{मुझे यह गाना अच्छा लगता है|mujhe yah gānā achchhā lagtā hai}} “I like this song”. Here {{अच्छा|achchhā}} and {{लगता|lagtā}} agree with the thing: {{मुझे चाय अच्छी लगती है|mujhe chāy achchhī lagtī hai}}.

ex.t: मेरी बेटी को चॉकलेट बहुत पसंद है।
ex.r: merī beṭī ko chôkleṭ bahut pasand hai.
ex.note: {{को|ko}} is a postposition, so a masculine word before it changes: {{मेरे बेटे को|mere beṭe ko}} “to my son” (lesson 9)

ex.t: उसे सुबह जल्दी उठना पसंद नहीं है।
ex.r: use subah jaldī uṭhnā pasand nahī̃ hai.
ex.tr: He doesn't like getting up early.

ex.t: हमें यहाँ रहना अच्छा लगता है।
ex.r: hamẽ yahā̃ rahnā achchhā lagtā hai.

ex.t: उन्हें क्रिकेट देखना बहुत पसंद है।
ex.r: unhẽ krikeṭ dekhnā bahut pasand hai.

blocks.tip: To say you love something, add {{बहुत|bahut}}: {{मुझे यह बहुत पसंद है|mujhe yah bahut pasand hai}} “I love it”. (Love for a person is {{प्यार|pyār}}, a different word.)

mistakes.why: With {{पसंद है|pasand hai}}, the person is in the “to” form: {{मुझे|mujhe}}.
The verb agrees with what you like: films, {{हैं|haĩ}}.
{{चाय|chāy}} is feminine: {{अच्छी लगती|achchhī lagtī}}.

practice.why: The songs are what the sentence is about: {{हैं|haĩ}}.

practice.q: How do you say “I like swimming”?
options: {{मुझे तैरना पसंद है।|mujhe tairnā pasand hai.}}
{{मुझे तैरता पसंद है।|mujhe tairtā pasand hai.}}
{{मैं तैरना पसंद हूँ।|maĩ tairnā pasand hū̃.}}
practice.why: Liking an activity: the {{-ना|-nā}} form, and {{मुझे|mujhe}}.

practice.q: A friend invites you to a cricket match. Choose your replies.

options: हाँ, मुझे क्रिकेट बहुत पसंद है!
हाँ, मैं क्रिकेट बहुत पसंद है!
rs: hā̃, mujhe krikeṭ bahut pasand hai!
hā̃, maĩ krikeṭ bahut pasand hai!

practice.t: मेरी माँ बहुत अच्छा खाना ___ हैं।
practice.tr: My mother cooks really good food.
practice.r: merī mā̃ bahut achchhā khānā ___ haĩ.

practice.q: Your turn: say two things you like, and one thing you don't like doing.

answers.t: मुझे पढ़ना और संगीत सुनना पसंद है, लेकिन मुझे खाना बनाना पसंद नहीं है।
answers.r: mujhe paṛhnā aur saṅgīt sunnā pasand hai, lekin mujhe khānā banānā pasand nahī̃ hai.
answers.tr: I like reading and listening to music, but I don't like cooking.

answers.t: मुझे चाय बहुत अच्छी लगती है। मुझे सुबह जल्दी उठना पसंद नहीं है।
answers.r: mujhe chāy bahut achchhī lagtī hai. mujhe subah jaldī uṭhnā pasand nahī̃ hai.
answers.tr: I love tea. I don't like getting up early.

lessons.title: Say what's happening right now
lessons.summary: Say what you're doing at this moment: “I'm cooking”, “It's raining”, “What are you doing?”
lessons.topic: {{रहा / रही / रहे|rahā / rahī / rahe}} + {{हूँ / है / हैं|hū̃ / hai / haĩ}}: the present continuous

goal.t: मैं अभी खाना बना रहा हूँ।
goal.r: maĩ abhī khānā banā rahā hū̃.
goal.tr: I'm cooking right now.
goal.note: said by a man; a woman says {{बना रही हूँ|banā rahī hū̃}}

dialog.t: हैलो! तुम क्या कर रहे हो?
dialog.r: hailo! tum kyā kar rahe ho?

dialog.t: मैं पढ़ रहा हूँ, माँ। कल परीक्षा है।
dialog.r: maĩ paṛh rahā hū̃, mā̃. kal parīkshā hai.
dialog.tr: I'm studying, Mom. There's an exam tomorrow.

dialog.t: हाँ, बहुत बारिश हो रही है।
dialog.r: hā̃, bahut bārish ho rahī hai.

blocks.p: **Right now.** For what is happening at this moment, Hindi uses the stem, then {{रहा|rahā}}, then {{हूँ / है / हैं / हो|hū̃ / hai / haĩ / ho}}: {{मैं पढ़ रहा हूँ|maĩ paṛh rahā hū̃}} “I'm studying”. {{रहा|rahā}} changes like an adjective in {{-आ|-ā}}: {{रहा|rahā}} for a man, {{रही|rahī}} for a woman, {{रहे|rahe}} for plurals and for {{आप|āp}}, {{तुम|tum}}, {{हम|ham}}.

table: {{मैं जा रहा हूँ|maĩ jā rahā hū̃}}
{{मैं जा रही हूँ|maĩ jā rahī hū̃}}
{{आप जा रहे हैं|āp jā rahe haĩ}}
{{आप जा रही हैं|āp jā rahī haĩ}}
{{तुम जा रहे हो|tum jā rahe ho}}
{{तुम जा रही हो|tum jā rahī ho}}
{{वह जा रहा है|vah jā rahā hai}}
{{वह जा रही है|vah jā rahī hai}}
{{हम / वे जा रहे हैं|ham / ve jā rahe haĩ}}
{{हम / वे जा रही हैं|ham / ve jā rahī haĩ}}

blocks.p: **Now, or usually?** Compare {{मैं चाय पीता हूँ|maĩ chāy pītā hū̃}} “I drink tea” (as a habit, lesson 14) with {{मैं चाय पी रहा हूँ|maĩ chāy pī rahā hū̃}} “I'm drinking tea” (now). Like English, Hindi also uses this form for plans that are already fixed: {{हम कल दिल्ली जा रहे हैं|ham kal dillī jā rahe haĩ}} “We're going to Delhi tomorrow.”
**The weather.** “It's raining” is {{बारिश हो रही है|bārish ho rahī hai}}, word for word “rain is happening”. {{बारिश|bārish}} is feminine, so {{रही|rahī}}.

ex.t: बच्चे पार्क में खेल रहे हैं।
ex.r: bachche pārk mẽ khel rahe haĩ.
ex.tr: The children are playing in the park.

ex.t: वह फ़ोन पर बात कर रही है।
ex.r: vah fon par bāt kar rahī hai.

mistakes.why: Don't forget the {{हूँ|hū̃}} at the end.
A woman is speaking. A woman says {{रही|rahī}}.
{{बारिश|bārish}} is feminine.

practice.q: Your friend Meena is speaking. Choose the right form.
Which one means “I'm drinking tea (right now)”?
options: {{मैं चाय पी रहा हूँ।|maĩ chāy pī rahā hū̃.}}
{{मैं चाय पीता हूँ।|maĩ chāy pītā hū̃.}}
practice.why: Right now: the stem + {{रहा हूँ|rahā hū̃}}. {{पीता हूँ|pītā hū̃}} is a habit.

practice.tr: The children are playing in the park.

practice.q: Your friend calls. Choose your replies (you're a man).

lines.why: Right now: {{बना रहा हूँ|banā rahā hū̃}}.

lines.t: अच्छा! क्या तुम्हें खाना बनाना पसंद है?
lines.r: achchhā! kyā tumhẽ khānā banānā pasand hai?

options: हाँ, मुझे खाना बनाना बहुत पसंद है।
हाँ, मैं खाना बनाना बहुत पसंद हूँ।
rs: hā̃, mujhe khānā banānā bahut pasand hai.
hā̃, maĩ khānā banānā bahut pasand hū̃.

practice.q: Your turn: someone calls and asks {{क्या कर रहे हो?|kyā kar rahe ho?}} Say what you and someone near you are doing.

answers.t: मैं हिंदी सीख रहा हूँ, और मेरी पत्नी किताब पढ़ रही है।
answers.r: maĩ hindī sīkh rahā hū̃, aur merī patnī kitāb paṛh rahī hai.
answers.tr: I'm learning Hindi, and my wife is reading a book.

answers.t: मैं कॉफ़ी पी रही हूँ, और बच्चे सो रहे हैं।
answers.r: maĩ kôfī pī rahī hū̃, aur bachche so rahe haĩ.
answers.tr: I'm having a coffee, and the children are sleeping.

lessons.title: Tell the time and say when
lessons.summary: Ask and tell the time, and say when things happen: “at half past six”, “on Monday”, “in the evening”.
lessons.topic: {{बजे|baje}} “o'clock, at … o'clock”; {{सवा|savā}}, {{साढ़े|sāṛhe}}, {{पौने|paune}}, {{डेढ़|ḍeṛh}}, {{ढाई|ḍhāī}}; {{को|ko}} with days and parts of the day

goal.t: फ़िल्म साढ़े छह बजे शुरू होती है।
goal.r: film sāṛhe chhah baje shurū hotī hai.
goal.tr: The movie starts at half past six.

dialog.tr: Excuse me, what time is it?

dialog.t: साढ़े पाँच बजे। और शनिवार को दो बजे।
dialog.r: sāṛhe pā̃ch baje. aur shanivār ko do baje.
dialog.tr: At half past five. And on Saturdays at two.

blocks.p: **What time is it?** {{कितने बजे हैं?|kitne baje haĩ?}} (people also say {{टाइम क्या हुआ है?|ṭāim kyā huā hai?}}). The answer is the number + {{बजे हैं|baje haĩ}}: {{तीन बजे हैं|tīn baje haĩ}} “It's three o'clock”. For one o'clock, {{एक बजा है|ek bajā hai}}.
**At what time?** “At” needs no word of its own: {{सात बजे|sāt baje}} is “at seven”. {{मैं सात बजे उठता हूँ|maĩ sāt baje uṭhtā hū̃}} “I get up at seven”.

**Quarters and halves.** Hindi has its own words: {{सवा|savā}} “a quarter past”, {{साढ़े|sāṛhe}} “half past”, {{पौने|paune}} “a quarter to”. And two special words: {{डेढ़|ḍeṛh}} is half past one and {{ढाई|ḍhāī}} half past two.

**Days, and parts of the day,** take {{को|ko}} for “on” or “in”: {{सोमवार को|somvār ko}} “on Monday”, {{शाम को|shām ko}} “in the evening”, {{रात को|rāt ko}} “at night”. {{सुबह|subah}} “in the morning” usually goes without it.

ex.t: मैं हर दिन सात बजे उठती हूँ।
ex.r: maĩ har din sāt baje uṭhtī hū̃.
ex.tr: I get up at seven every day.

ex.t: दुकान रात दस बजे तक खुली है।
ex.r: dukān rāt das baje tak khulī hai.
ex.tr: The shop is open until ten at night.

ex.t: हम शनिवार को बाज़ार जाते हैं।
ex.r: ham shanivār ko bāzār jāte haĩ.
ex.tr: We go to the market on Saturdays.

ex.t: ट्रेन पौने नौ बजे आती है।
ex.r: ṭren paune nau baje ātī hai.
ex.tr: The train comes at a quarter to nine.

ex.t: वह शाम को योग करती है।
ex.r: vah shām ko yog kartī hai.
ex.tr: She does yoga in the evening.

mistakes.wrong: मैं साढ़े एक बजे खाना खाता हूँ।
mistakes.right: मैं डेढ़ बजे खाना खाता हूँ।
mistakes.tr: I have lunch at half past one.
mistakes.why: Half past one is {{डेढ़|ḍeṛh}}, never {{साढ़े एक|sāṛhe ek}}.

mistakes.wrong: मैं सात बजे पर उठता हूँ।
mistakes.why: “At seven” is just {{सात बजे|sāt baje}}: no {{पर|par}}.

practice.q: What time is {{साढ़े तीन बजे|sāṛhe tīn baje}}?

practice.why: Half past two has its own word: {{ढाई|ḍhāī}}.

practice.tr: We go to the market on Saturdays.
The train comes at a quarter to nine.

practice.q: Making a plan on the phone. Choose your replies.

lines.why: No word for “at”: just the time and {{बजे|baje}}.

lines.t: ठीक है। हम कहाँ मिल रहे हैं?
lines.r: ṭhīk hai. ham kahā̃ mil rahe haĩ?

lines.why: The postposition comes after the noun.

practice.q: Your turn: say what time you get up, and what you do on Saturdays.

answers.t: मैं साढ़े छह बजे उठता हूँ। शनिवार को मैं दोस्तों के साथ क्रिकेट खेलता हूँ।
answers.r: maĩ sāṛhe chhah baje uṭhtā hū̃. shanivār ko maĩ dostõ ke sāth krikeṭ kheltā hū̃.
answers.tr: I get up at half past six. On Saturdays I play cricket with friends. (a man)

answers.t: मैं सात बजे उठती हूँ, और शनिवार को मैं बाज़ार जाती हूँ।
answers.r: maĩ sāt baje uṭhtī hū̃, aur shanivār ko maĩ bāzār jātī hū̃.
answers.tr: I get up at seven, and on Saturdays I go to the market. (a woman)

lessons.title: Say where you were and what it was like
lessons.summary: Talk about the past for the first time: “I was at home yesterday”, “The food was really good.”
lessons.topic: {{था / थी / थे / थीं|thā / thī / the / thī̃}} “was, were”

goal.t: कल मैं घर पर था। मौसम बहुत ख़राब था।
goal.r: kal maĩ ghar par thā. mausam bahut kharāb thā.
goal.tr: Yesterday I was at home. The weather was really bad.
goal.note: said by a man; a woman says {{मैं घर पर थी|maĩ ghar par thī}}

dialog.t: मैं आगरा में था, दोस्तों के साथ।
dialog.r: maĩ āgrā mẽ thā, dostõ ke sāth.
dialog.tr: I was in Agra, with friends.

dialog.t: बहुत सुंदर! लेकिन वहाँ बहुत भीड़ थी।
dialog.r: bahut sundar! lekin vahā̃ bahut bhīṛ thī.
dialog.tr: Really beautiful! But it was very crowded.
The food was really good too.

blocks.p: **Was and were.** The past of {{है|hai}} is {{था|thā}}, and it changes like an adjective in {{-आ|-ā}}: for masculine or feminine, one or more. It does *not* change for “I”, “you” or “he”, as {{हूँ, है, हो|hū̃, hai, ho}} do.

table: more than one, or {{आप, तुम, हम|āp, tum, ham}}

blocks.p: {{मैं घर पर था|maĩ ghar par thā}} “I was at home” (a man), {{मैं घर पर थी|maĩ ghar par thī}} (a woman); {{आप कहाँ थे?|āp kahā̃ the?}} “Where were you?”; {{वे लोग बहुत अच्छे थे|ve log bahut achchhe the}} “Those people were very nice”; {{दुकानें बंद थीं|dukānẽ band thī̃}} “The shops were closed”.

**Time words for the past**: {{कल|kal}} “yesterday” (it also means “tomorrow”: the verb tells you which!), {{पिछले हफ़्ते|pichhle hafte}} “last week”, {{पहले|pahle}} “before, in the past”. Like all time words, they come early in the sentence.

**There was, I had.** Everything you built with {{है|hai}} works with {{था|thā}}: {{वहाँ बहुत भीड़ थी|vahā̃ bahut bhīṛ thī}} “There was a big crowd there”, {{मेरे पास समय नहीं था|mere pās samay nahī̃ thā}} “I didn't have time”.

ex.tr: There were a lot of people at the party.

mistakes.why: For the past, {{था|thā}} takes the place of {{हूँ|hū̃}}.
A woman is speaking. A woman says {{थी|thī}}.
Feminine plural: {{थीं|thī̃}}.

practice.tr: There were a lot of people at the party.

options: yesterday or tomorrow: the verb tells you which
practice.why: {{कल मैं घर पर था|kal maĩ ghar par thā}}: yesterday. With a verb about the future (lesson 21), tomorrow.

practice.q: A colleague asks about your weekend. Choose your replies (you're a woman).
Ask your friend Raj: “Where were you yesterday?”
Your turn: say where you were last weekend, and what it was like.

answers.t: पिछले हफ़्ते मैं मुंबई में था। मौसम बहुत गरम था, लेकिन खाना बहुत अच्छा था।
answers.r: pichhle hafte maĩ mumbaī mẽ thā. mausam bahut garam thā, lekin khānā bahut achchhā thā.
answers.tr: Last week I was in Mumbai. The weather was very hot, but the food was great.

answers.t: शनिवार को मैं एक शादी में थी। बहुत लोग थे और खाना बहुत अच्छा था।
answers.r: shanivār ko maĩ ek shādī mẽ thī. bahut log the aur khānā bahut achchhā thā.
answers.tr: On Saturday I was at a wedding. There were lots of people and the food was great.

lessons.title: Say what you want to do
lessons.summary: Say “I want to learn Hindi”, “I want to go to Goa”, and ask what others want to do.
lessons.topic: {{चाहना|chāhnā}} “to want” + the {{-ना|-nā}} form; {{चाहिए|chāhie}} or {{चाहना|chāhnā}}?

goal.t: मैं हिंदी सीखना चाहता हूँ।
goal.r: maĩ hindī sīkhnā chāhtā hū̃.
goal.tr: I want to learn Hindi.
goal.note: said by a man; a woman says {{चाहती हूँ|chāhtī hū̃}}

dialog.t: तुम छुट्टियों में क्या करना चाहती हो?
dialog.r: tum chhuṭṭiyõ mẽ kyā karnā chāhtī ho?
dialog.tr: What do you want to do on vacation?

dialog.t: मैं गोवा जाना चाहती हूँ। मैं समुद्र देखना चाहती हूँ।
dialog.r: maĩ govā jānā chāhtī hū̃. maĩ samudra dekhnā chāhtī hū̃.
dialog.tr: I want to go to Goa. I want to see the ocean.

dialog.t: वह कुछ नहीं करना चाहता। वह बस सोना चाहता है!
dialog.r: vah kuchh nahī̃ karnā chāhtā. vah bas sonā chāhtā hai!
dialog.tr: He doesn't want to do anything. He just wants to sleep!

blocks.p: **Want to do.** {{चाहना|chāhnā}} “to want” is an ordinary verb, with the present endings of lesson 14: {{मैं चाहता हूँ|maĩ chāhtā hū̃}} (a man), {{मैं चाहती हूँ|maĩ chāhtī hū̃}} (a woman). What you want to do goes before it, in the {{-ना|-nā}} form: {{मैं गोवा जाना चाहती हूँ|maĩ govā jānā chāhtī hū̃}} “I want to go to Goa”, word for word “I Goa to-go want”.

**Two ways of wanting.** {{मुझे … चाहिए|mujhe … chāhie}} (lesson 4) is for things you need or ask for: {{मुझे चाय चाहिए|mujhe chāy chāhie}}. {{चाहना|chāhnā}} is for what you want to do: {{मैं चाय पीना चाहता हूँ|maĩ chāy pīnā chāhtā hū̃}} “I want to drink tea”. With {{चाहना|chāhnā}}, the person is the ordinary {{मैं|maĩ}}, not {{मुझे|mujhe}}.

table: {{मुझे एक टिकट चाहिए।|mujhe ek ṭikaṭ chāhie.}}
{{मैं घर जाना चाहता हूँ।|maĩ ghar jānā chāhtā hū̃.}}
{{आप क्या खाना चाहेंगे?|āp kyā khānā chāhẽge?}}
What would you like to eat?

blocks.p: **Polite offers.** Waiters and hosts use the future of {{चाहना|chāhnā}}, {{चाहेंगे|chāhẽge}}, for “would you like”: {{आप क्या लेना चाहेंगे?|āp kyā lenā chāhẽge?}} “What would you like to have?” (The future is the next lesson.)

ex.t: मैं हिंदी अच्छी तरह बोलना चाहता हूँ।
ex.r: maĩ hindī achchhī tarah bolnā chāhtā hū̃.
ex.tr: I want to speak Hindi well.
She wants to become a doctor.

ex.t: क्या तुम मेरे साथ आना चाहते हो?
ex.r: kyā tum mere sāth ānā chāhte ho?
ex.tr: Do you want to come with me?
We want to travel around India.

ex.t: मैं आज कुछ नहीं करना चाहती।
ex.r: maĩ āj kuchh nahī̃ karnā chāhtī.
ex.tr: I don't want to do anything today.
ex.note: a woman speaking; the {{हूँ|hū̃}} is left out after {{नहीं|nahī̃}} (lesson 15)

ex.tr: The children want to play outside.

blocks.tip: In a shop or a café, {{मैं … चाहता हूँ|maĩ … chāhtā hū̃}} can sound a little blunt; there, {{मुझे … चाहिए|mujhe … chāhie}} or {{… दीजिए|… dījie}} is more natural.

mistakes.why: With {{चाहना|chāhnā}}, the person is {{मैं|maĩ}}. {{मुझे|mujhe}} goes with {{चाहिए|chāhie}}.
The verb before {{चाहना|chāhnā}} is in its {{-ना|-nā}} form.

practice.tr: I want to go to Goa.

practice.q: Which one is right for “I want to drink water”?
options: {{मैं पानी पीना चाहता हूँ।|maĩ pānī pīnā chāhtā hū̃.}}
{{मुझे पानी पीना चाहता हूँ।|mujhe pānī pīnā chāhtā hū̃.}}
practice.why: With {{चाहना|chāhnā}}: {{मैं|maĩ}}. ({{मुझे पानी चाहिए|mujhe pānī chāhie}} would be “I need water”.)

practice.q: Your friend Anil is speaking. Choose the right form.
practice.tr: I want to become a doctor.
Do you want to come with me?

lines.r: shanivār ko kyā karnā chāhtī ho?
lines.tr: What do you want to do on Saturday?

options: कोई भी! मैं बस घर से बाहर जाना चाहती हूँ।
कोई भी! मुझे बस घर से बाहर जाना चाहती हूँ।
rs: koī bhī! maĩ bas ghar se bāhar jānā chāhtī hū̃.
koī bhī! mujhe bas ghar se bāhar jānā chāhtī hū̃.

practice.q: Say: “The children want to play outside.”
Your turn: say two things you want to do this year.

answers.t: मैं हिंदी सीखना चाहता हूँ और भारत जाना चाहता हूँ।
answers.r: maĩ hindī sīkhnā chāhtā hū̃ aur bhārat jānā chāhtā hū̃.
answers.tr: I want to learn Hindi and go to India. (a man)

answers.t: मैं ज़्यादा पढ़ना चाहती हूँ, और रोज़ योग करना चाहती हूँ।
answers.r: maĩ zyādā paṛhnā chāhtī hū̃, aur roz yog karnā chāhtī hū̃.
answers.tr: I want to read more, and do yoga every day. (a woman)

lessons.title: Say what you will do
lessons.summary: Talk about tomorrow and next week: “I'll call you”, “It'll rain”, “We'll go to Delhi.”
lessons.topic: The future: {{-ऊँगा|-ū̃gā}}, {{-एगा|-egā}}, {{-ओगे|-oge}}, {{-एँगे|-ẽge}} (and {{-गी|-gī}} for women); {{होगा|hogā}} “will be”

goal.t: कल मैं तुम्हें फ़ोन करूँगा।
goal.r: kal maĩ tumhẽ fon karū̃gā.
goal.tr: I'll call you tomorrow.
goal.note: said by a man; a woman says {{करूँगी|karū̃gī}}

dialog.t: सुबह मैं जिम जाऊँगा, फिर शाम को दोस्तों से मिलूँगा।
dialog.r: subah maĩ jim jāū̃gā, phir shām ko dostõ se milū̃gā.
dialog.tr: In the morning I'll go to the gym, then in the evening I'll meet friends.
It's going to rain tomorrow, you know?

dialog.t: तो मैं घर पर रहूँगा और फ़िल्म देखूँगा!
dialog.r: to maĩ ghar par rahū̃gā aur film dekhū̃gā!
dialog.tr: Then I'll stay home and watch a movie!

blocks.p: **The future.** Take the stem and add one ending that says who, then {{-गा|-gā}}, {{-गी|-gī}} or {{-गे|-ge}} for masculine, feminine or plural. There is no {{हूँ|hū̃}} or {{है|hai}} at the end: the ending does all the work.

Every verb takes the same endings: {{करूँगा|karū̃gā}} “I'll do”, {{खाएगी|khāegī}} “she'll eat”, {{देखेंगे|dekhẽge}} “we'll see”. Two common verbs are shorter: {{देना|denā}} → {{दूँगा|dū̃gā}}, {{देगा|degā}}, {{देंगे|dẽge}} “will give”; {{लेना|lenā}} → {{लूँगा|lū̃gā}}, {{लेगा|legā}}, {{लेंगे|lẽge}} “will take”.

**Will be.** The future of {{होना|honā}} “to be” is {{होगा|hogā}}, {{होगी|hogī}}, {{होंगे|hõge}}: {{कल बारिश होगी|kal bārish hogī}} “It'll rain tomorrow”, {{पार्टी बहुत अच्छी होगी|pārṭī bahut achchhī hogī}} “The party will be great”.

**Time words** for the future: {{कल|kal}} “tomorrow” (with a future verb, it can't be “yesterday”), {{परसों|parsõ}} “the day after tomorrow”, {{अगले हफ़्ते|agle hafte}} “next week”, {{बाद में|bād mẽ}} “later”.

ex.tr: We'll go to Delhi next week.

ex.t: मैं तुम्हें बाद में फ़ोन करूँगा।
ex.r: maĩ tumhẽ bād mẽ fon karū̃gā.

ex.t: आप क्या लेंगे, चाय या कॉफ़ी?
ex.r: āp kyā lẽge, chāy yā kôfī?
ex.tr: What will you have, tea or coffee?

blocks.tip: Hindi also uses {{होगा|hogā}} for a guess about now: {{वह घर पर होगा|vah ghar par hogā}} “He must be at home” (lesson 48).

mistakes.why: The future has no {{हूँ|hū̃}} or {{है|hai}} at the end.
A woman is speaking: the ending is {{-गी|-gī}}.
{{हम|ham}} “we”: {{-एँगे|-ẽge}}.

practice.tr: We'll go to Delhi next week.

practice.q: A woman is speaking. Choose the right form.
Making plans. Choose your replies (you're a man).

options: दस बजे। मैं तुम्हें फ़ोन करूँगा।
दस बजे पर। मैं तुम्हें फ़ोन करूँगा।
rs: das baje. maĩ tumhẽ fon karū̃gā.
das baje par. maĩ tumhẽ fon karū̃gā.

practice.q: Ask your friend Sam: “What will you do tomorrow?”
Your turn: say three things you'll do this weekend.

answers.t: शनिवार को मैं देर से उठूँगा, फिर दोस्तों से मिलूँगा।
answers.r: shanivār ko maĩ der se uṭhū̃gā, phir dostõ se milū̃gā.
answers.tr: On Saturday I'll get up late, then meet friends. (a man)

answers.t: रविवार को मैं खाना बनाऊँगी और एक किताब पढ़ूँगी।
answers.r: ravivār ko maĩ khānā banāū̃gī aur ek kitāb paṛhū̃gī.
answers.tr: On Sunday I'll cook and read a book. (a woman)

lessons.title: Say what you can and can't do
lessons.summary: Say “I can swim”, ask “May I sit here?” and “Could you help me?”, and say which languages you know.
lessons.topic: {{सकना|saknā}} “can” after the stem; asking permission; {{मुझे हिंदी आती है|mujhe hindī ātī hai}} “I know Hindi”; {{पाना|pānā}} “manage to”

goal.t: क्या मैं यहाँ बैठ सकता हूँ?
goal.r: kyā maĩ yahā̃ baiṭh saktā hū̃?
goal.tr: May I sit here?
goal.note: said by a man; a woman says {{सकती हूँ|saktī hū̃}}

dialog.t: माफ़ कीजिए, क्या मैं यहाँ बैठ सकता हूँ?
dialog.r: māf kījie, kyā maĩ yahā̃ baiṭh saktā hū̃?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, may I sit here?

dialog.t: हाँ, बैठिए। आप हिंदी बोल सकते हैं!
dialog.r: hā̃, baiṭhie. āp hindī bol sakte haĩ!
dialog.tr: Yes, sit down. You can speak Hindi!

dialog.t: थोड़ी-थोड़ी। मुझे हिंदी थोड़ी आती है।
dialog.r: thoṛī-thoṛī. mujhe hindī thoṛī ātī hai.
dialog.tr: A little. I know a little Hindi.

dialog.t: बहुत अच्छे! क्या आप हिंदी पढ़ सकते हैं?
dialog.r: bahut achchhe! kyā āp hindī paṛh sakte haĩ?
dialog.tr: Very good! Can you read Hindi?

dialog.t: अभी नहीं, लेकिन मैं सीख रहा हूँ।
dialog.r: abhī nahī̃, lekin maĩ sīkh rahā hū̃.

blocks.p: **Can.** {{सकना|saknā}} “to be able” comes after the stem of the main verb, and takes the endings: {{मैं हिंदी बोल सकता हूँ|maĩ hindī bol saktā hū̃}} “I can speak Hindi”, {{वह तैर सकती है|vah tair saktī hai}} “She can swim”. The main verb is just its stem and never changes.

table: {{मैं आ सकता हूँ।|maĩ ā saktā hū̃.}}
{{मैं नहीं आ सकता।|maĩ nahī̃ ā saktā.}}

blocks.p: **May I? Could you?** A question with {{सकना|saknā}} asks for permission: {{क्या मैं अंदर आ सकता हूँ?|kyā maĩ andar ā saktā hū̃?}} “May I come in?” With {{आप|āp}}, it is a polite request: {{क्या आप थोड़ा धीरे बोल सकते हैं?|kyā āp thoṛā dhīre bol sakte haĩ?}} “Could you speak a little slower?”

**Knowing a language or a skill.** For something you have learned, Hindi likes the “to” form with {{आना|ānā}} “to come”: {{मुझे हिंदी आती है|mujhe hindī ātī hai}} “I know Hindi”, word for word “Hindi comes to me”; {{मुझे तैरना आता है|mujhe tairnā ātā hai}} “I know how to swim”. The verb agrees with the language or the skill: {{हिंदी|hindī}} is feminine, so {{आती|ātī}}.

**Manage to.** {{पाना|pānā}} works like {{सकना|saknā}} but means “manage to”, and is very common with {{नहीं|nahī̃}}: {{मैं रात को ठीक से सो नहीं पाता|maĩ rāt ko ṭhīk se so nahī̃ pātā}} “I can't manage to sleep properly at night”, {{मैं कल नहीं आ पाऊँगी|maĩ kal nahī̃ ā pāū̃gī}} “I won't be able to make it tomorrow”.

ex.t: क्या आप मेरी मदद कर सकते हैं?
ex.r: kyā āp merī madad kar sakte haĩ?
ex.note: {{मदद|madad}} “help” is feminine, so “my help” is {{मेरी मदद|merī madad}}

ex.t: क्या यहाँ फ़ोटो ले सकते हैं?
ex.r: kyā yahā̃ foṭo le sakte haĩ?

ex.t: वह बहुत अच्छा गा सकती है।
ex.r: vah bahut achchhā gā saktī hai.

mistakes.why: Before {{सकना|saknā}}, only the stem: {{बोल|bol}}, not {{बोलना|bolnā}}.
Knowing a language is “Hindi comes to me”: {{मुझे … आती है|mujhe … ātī hai}}.

practice.t: क्या आप मेरी मदद कर ___ हैं?
practice.r: kyā āp merī madad kar ___ haĩ?

options: {{मैं नहीं आ सकता।|maĩ nahī̃ ā saktā.}}
{{मैं आना नहीं सकता।|maĩ ānā nahī̃ saktā.}}
{{मुझे नहीं आ सकता।|mujhe nahī̃ ā saktā.}}

“Hindi comes to me”, and {{हिंदी|hindī}} is feminine: {{आती|ātī}}.

practice.q: In a clothing store: choose your lines (you're a man).

क्या मैं यह शर्ट देखना सकता हूँ?
rs: kyā maĩ yah sharṭ dekh saktā hū̃?
kyā maĩ yah sharṭ dekhnā saktā hū̃?

शुक्रिया। क्या मैं कार्ड से पैसे दे सकता हैं?
rs: shukriyā. kyā maĩ kārḍ se paise de saktā hū̃?

practice.answer: क्या आप थोड़ा धीरे बोल सकते हैं?
practice.r: kyā āp thoṛā dhīre bol sakte haĩ?

practice.q: Your turn: say two things you can do, one you can't, and which languages you know.

answers.t: मैं तैर सकता हूँ और गाड़ी चला सकता हूँ, लेकिन मैं नाच नहीं सकता। मुझे अंग्रेज़ी और थोड़ी हिंदी आती है।

answers.tr: I know Spanish. I can cook, but I can't sing. (a woman)

lessons.title: Say what you have to do and should do
lessons.summary: Say “I have to get up early”, “You should rest”, “We'll have to wait”: three ways of saying must.
lessons.topic: The “to” form + the {{-ना|-nā}} form + {{है|hai}} (have to), {{चाहिए|chāhie}} (should), {{पड़ेगा|paṛegā}} (will have to)

goal.t: मुझे कल जल्दी उठना है।
goal.r: mujhe kal jaldī uṭhnā hai.
goal.tr: I have to get up early tomorrow.

dialog.tr: Are you coming to the party tonight?

dialog.t: नहीं यार, मुझे कल जल्दी उठना है। मुझे सुबह छह बजे एयरपोर्ट जाना है।
dialog.r: nahī̃ yār, mujhe kal jaldī uṭhnā hai. mujhe subah chhah baje eyarporṭ jānā hai.
dialog.tr: No, man, I have to get up early tomorrow. I have to go to the airport at six in the morning.

dialog.t: अरे! फिर तुम्हें जल्दी सोना चाहिए।
dialog.r: are! phir tumhẽ jaldī sonā chāhie.
dialog.tr: Oh! Then you should go to bed early.

dialog.t: हाँ। और मुझे अभी सामान भी पैक करना पड़ेगा!
dialog.r: hā̃. aur mujhe abhī sāmān bhī paik karnā paṛegā!
dialog.tr: Yes. And I'll have to pack my bags right now too!

blocks.p: **Three kinds of “have to”.** All three put the person in the “to” form (lesson 16) and the action in the {{-ना|-nā}} form; only the last word changes:

table: I have to go; I'm going to go (a plan, a task)

blocks.p: **{{है|hai}}: I've got to.** {{मुझे काम करना है|mujhe kām karnā hai}} “I have to work” is the everyday way to say what you have to do or plan to do. Its past is {{मुझे जाना था|mujhe jānā thā}} “I was supposed to go”.

**{{चाहिए|chāhie}}: should.** The same {{चाहिए|chāhie}} as “I need” (lesson 4), but after a verb it means “should”: {{आपको आराम करना चाहिए|āpko ārām karnā chāhie}} “You should rest.” It never changes.

**{{पड़ना|paṛnā}}: must, with no choice.** {{पड़ना|paṛnā}} (literally “to fall”) is for things you can't avoid: {{मुझे रोज़ बस से जाना पड़ता है|mujhe roz bas se jānā paṛtā hai}} “I have to take the bus every day (there's no other way)”. It takes the ordinary tenses: {{पड़ता है|paṛtā hai}} (usually), {{पड़ेगा|paṛegā}} (will have to).

ex.t: मुझे डॉक्टर के पास जाना है।
ex.r: mujhe ḍôkṭar ke pās jānā hai.
ex.tr: I have to go to the doctor.
We'll have to go to the office tomorrow.

ex.t: उसे रोज़ बहुत दूर जाना पड़ता है।
ex.r: use roz bahut dūr jānā paṛtā hai.
ex.tr: She has to travel a long way every day.
Children should go to bed early.
ex.note: {{बच्चों को|bachchõ ko}}: before {{को|ko}}, the plural ends in {{-ओं|-õ}} (lesson 9)

blocks.tip: Hindi speakers often make the {{-ना|-nā}} form agree with a feminine thing: {{मुझे चाय पीनी है|mujhe chāy pīnī hai}} “I want to have some tea”, {{तुम्हें हिंदी फ़िल्में देखनी चाहिए|tumhẽ hindī filmẽ dekhnī chāhie}} “You should watch Hindi films”. You'll hear both {{पीना|pīnā}} and {{पीनी|pīnī}}; both are understood.

mistakes.why: “Have to” uses the “to” form: {{मुझे|mujhe}}.
{{चाहिए|chāhie}} “should” needs the “to” form too: {{तुम्हें|tumhẽ}}.

lessons.title: Make suggestions and offers
lessons.summary: Say “Shall we go?”, “Let's eat out”, “Shall I help?”, “What should I do?”, and “maybe”.
lessons.topic: The subjunctive: {{चलें?|chalẽ?}}, {{करूँ?|karū̃?}}; {{चलो|chalo}} “let's”; {{शायद|shāyad}} “maybe” + the subjunctive

goal.t: चलो, आज बाहर खाएँ?
goal.r: chalo, āj bāhar khāẽ?
goal.tr: Come on, shall we eat out today?

dialog.tr: What shall we do this evening?

dialog.t: नहीं, चलो बाहर खाएँ। आज मैं खाना नहीं बनाना चाहती।
dialog.r: nahī̃, chalo bāhar khāẽ. āj maĩ khānā nahī̃ banānā chāhtī.
dialog.tr: No, let's eat out. I don't want to cook today.
OK. Shall I call a taxi?

dialog.t: नहीं, पैदल चलते हैं। पास में ही है।
dialog.r: nahī̃, paidal chalte haĩ. pās mẽ hī hai.
dialog.tr: No, let's walk. It's close by.

blocks.means: a verb form for what might, could or should happen, rather than what does: “shall we go?”, “maybe she'll come”, “I want you to come”.

blocks.p: **Shall we? Shall I?** The subjunctive is the future (lesson 21) without its {{-गा|-gā}}: {{जाएँगे|jāẽge}} “we'll go” → {{जाएँ|jāẽ}} “shall we go?”; {{करूँगा|karū̃gā}} “I'll do” → {{करूँ|karū̃}} “shall I do?” In a question it makes a suggestion or an offer: {{हम चलें?|ham chalẽ?}} “Shall we go?”, {{मैं मदद करूँ?|maĩ madad karū̃?}} “Shall I help?”
Without its {{-गा|-gā}}, it no longer changes for masculine or feminine: {{मैं क्या करूँ?|maĩ kyā karū̃?}} “What shall I do?” is the same for a man and a woman.

**Let's.** Start with {{चलो|chalo}} (to friends) or {{चलिए|chalie}} (politely), literally “come on”: {{चलो, घर चलें|chalo, ghar chalẽ}} “Come on, let's go home”. In everyday speech people also say “let's” with the plain present: {{चलो, घर चलते हैं|chalo, ghar chalte haĩ}}.
**Maybe.** {{शायद|shāyad}} “perhaps” is often followed by the subjunctive: {{शायद वह आए|shāyad vah āe}} “Maybe he'll come (he might come)”.

ex.tr: Come on, let's have some tea.

ex.note: with {{आप|āp}}, the subjunctive is an even politer request than {{बैठिए|baiṭhie}}

blocks.tip: On signs and in announcements you'll see the polite {{आप|āp}} form without {{आप|āp}}: {{कृपया शांत रहें|kripayā shānt rahẽ}} “Please be quiet”.

mistakes.why: With {{मैं|maĩ}}, the subjunctive ends in {{-ऊँ|-ū̃}}: {{करूँ|karū̃}}.
The subjunctive needs no {{हूँ|hū̃}}.

lessons.title: Make plans with a friend
lessons.summary: Invite someone, agree on a time, and say what you're going to do: “I'll come and pick you up.”
lessons.topic: The future and the subjunctive together; {{-ने|-ne}} + {{आना / जाना|ānā / jānā}} for “come / go and do”

goal.t: मैं शनिवार को तुम्हारे घर खाना खाने आऊँगा।
goal.r: maĩ shanivār ko tumhāre ghar khānā khāne āū̃gā.
goal.tr: I'll come to your place for dinner on Saturday.
goal.note: said by a man; a woman says {{आऊँगी|āū̃gī}}

dialog.t: हैलो! इस शनिवार को तुम क्या कर रहे हो?
dialog.r: hailo! is shanivār ko tum kyā kar rahe ho?
dialog.tr: Hello! What are you doing this Saturday?

dialog.t: हम लोग बाज़ार घूमने जा रहे हैं। तुम भी चलोगे?
dialog.r: ham log bāzār ghūmne jā rahe haĩ. tum bhī chaloge?
dialog.tr: We're going to look around the market. Will you come too?
Sure! What time shall we meet?

dialog.t: ग्यारह बजे? मैं तुम्हें लेने आऊँगी।
dialog.r: gyārah baje? maĩ tumhẽ lene āū̃gī.
dialog.tr: Eleven? I'll come and pick you up.

dialog.t: बढ़िया। फिर दोपहर को कहीं खाना खाएँगे।
dialog.r: baṛhiyā. phir dopahar ko kahī̃ khānā khāẽge.
dialog.tr: Great. Then we'll eat somewhere at lunchtime.

blocks.p: This conversation uses almost everything from this unit: the future ({{चलोगे?|chaloge?}} “will you come?”), the present continuous for a fixed plan ({{जा रहे हैं|jā rahe haĩ}}, lesson 17) and the subjunctive for a suggestion ({{कितने बजे मिलें?|kitne baje milẽ?}}). One new thing makes plans easy:

**Come or go and do something.** With {{आना|ānā}} “to come” and {{जाना|jānā}} “to go”, say what for with the {{-ने|-ne}} form of the verb (the {{-ना|-nā}} form, with the {{-ए|-e}} of the oblique, lesson 9): {{मैं तुम्हें लेने आऊँगी|maĩ tumhẽ lene āū̃gī}} “I'll come and pick you up”, {{हम घूमने जा रहे हैं|ham ghūmne jā rahe haĩ}} “We're going (out) to look around”. No word for “to” is needed.

table: {{मैं दोस्तों से मिलने जा रहा हूँ।|maĩ dostõ se milne jā rahā hū̃.}}
{{हम सब्ज़ी ख़रीदने बाज़ार जाते हैं।|ham sabzī kharīdne bāzār jāte haĩ.}}
We go to the market to buy vegetables.

blocks.p: **Inviting and answering.** To invite: {{तुम भी चलोगे?|tum bhī chaloge?}} or {{आप भी चलेंगे?|āp bhī chalẽge?}} “Will you come too?” To say yes: {{ज़रूर!|zarūr!}} “Sure!”, {{ठीक है|ṭhīk hai}} “OK”. To say no kindly: {{माफ़ कीजिए, मैं नहीं आ पाऊँगा|māf kījie, maĩ nahī̃ ā pāū̃gā}} “Sorry, I won't be able to come” (lesson 22).

ex.tr: We're going on a picnic tomorrow.

ex.t: मैं तुम्हें स्टेशन पर लेने आऊँगा।
ex.r: maĩ tumhẽ sṭeshan par lene āū̃gā.
ex.tr: I'll come and pick you up at the station.

ex.t: आप रविवार को खाना खाने आइए।
ex.r: āp ravivār ko khānā khāne āie.

ex.t: वे फ़िल्म देखने जा रहे हैं।
ex.r: ve film dekhne jā rahe haĩ.
ex.tr: They're going to see a movie.

ex.t: माफ़ कीजिए, मैं नहीं आ पाऊँगी।
ex.r: māf kījie, maĩ nahī̃ ā pāū̃gī.
ex.tr: Sorry, I won't be able to come.

mistakes.why: With {{आना|ānā}} and {{जाना|jānā}}, the purpose takes {{-ने|-ne}}: {{लेने|lene}}.
